Chapter 3: The Harsh Realities of Survival—Work, Exploitation, and the Search for Dignity.
For most of us, survival probably feels pretty ordinary. You get up, go to work, come home, and find comfort in what’s familiar. But imagine if you had to leave everything behind—your home, your friends, your whole world. Suddenly, survival means something totally different. It’s not about routine anymore. It’s about grabbing any job you can, often behind the scenes, always at the mercy of someone in charge.
And dignity? That becomes something you have to fight for, day after day. It’s not always about pride—it’s about not losing yourself when just getting by feels like the only thing that matters.
Picture the boy’s journey. He moves from one country to another, never finding solid ground. In one city, he lands a job at a brick factory. The air’s so thick with dust it’s hard to breathe, and the hours feel endless. The work is backbreaking, and the pay? Barely enough to scrape by. He figures out fast that complaining gets him nowhere. There are always others waiting to take his spot. The foreman barely notices him—he cares more about hitting numbers than the people doing the work.
The boy’s hands grow rough and calloused. His back aches from bending and lifting, day after day. And yet, there’s a strange sense of pride in it—he’s taking care of himself, not depending on anyone’s charity. There’s comfort in the small community he finds among the other workers. They share stories about where they came from, about families left behind, and dreams they still hold onto. In those moments, he feels like he belongs—at least for a little while.
But the truth is, life as an undocumented worker is tough. He’s always aware of his fragile situation. He gets paid less, given the worst jobs, and lives with the constant fear of being reported or sent away. Every conversation feels like it could be risky. So, he learns to be careful, only trusting people who’ve truly earned it.
But even in the toughest times, there are glimmers of kindness. Maybe a supervisor sneaks him an extra meal, or a coworker steps in to help with a tough job. These little moments lift him up—they show him that not everyone is indifferent. Still, for every act of kindness, there are plenty of times when things go the other way. Sometimes his pay is held back, or promises made to him are broken, leaving him feeling powerless all over again.
The search for dignity never stops. He wants more than just survival—he wants to be seen, to be respected. But in a world that chases profit over people, dignity is often the first thing lost. So he learns to celebrate small wins. A job done right, a shared laugh with a friend, or simply making it through another day—these become his victories.
It’s easy for most people to take their rights for granted—the right to work, to fair pay, to be treated with decency. But for those living in the shadows, these rights are out of reach, handed out or taken away on someone else’s whim.
The boy’s journey reminds us just how fragile dignity can be—and how fiercely it must be reclaimed, one day at a time.
